words: hola; adiós; ¿cómo te llamas?; me llamo; ¿cómo estás?; bien; mal; ¿qué te gusta?; me gusta; no me gusta; ¿cuándo es tu cumpleaños?; por favor; gracias; ¿cómo?; otra vez
cross_subject: ela:ek-discussion (taking turns and listening in a partner exchange)
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Function: greet and take leave, introduce self, ask and answer very predictable questions by naming, listing and identifying, and say what one likes. Themes: greetings and introductions; classroom and school things; numbers, days, months, dates and weather; likes and free time; describing a person or a character (colors, clothes, a few adjectives); a family, real or made up. Text type: single words, practiced phrases and a few memorized sentences, spoken and in short written chat lines. Grammar as chunks, not rules: me llamo, tengo ... años, me gusta / no me gusta with a noun or an infinitive, ¿te gusta...?, hay, es and son with an adjective, el and la noticed with each new noun, numbers 0 to 100. Accuracy: right on rehearsed chunks and falling off on anything new; the learner repairs with gesture, repetition and ¿Cómo? Otra vez, por favor. In each unit the learner does an information-gap exchange: each partner holds a card the other lacks (a class schedule, a birthday list, a weather map) and they ask until both cards are full, then report one fact. On the Check day the pair uses a new card neither has seen: rehearsed language, unrehearsed content. Heritage path: a learner who already does this orally does the exchange in writing, works on spelling and on usted for an adult, and is never the class model or the translator. Early-years companion (same target): greeting songs, circle and name games, puppets and pointing answers; the exchange is spoken (the companion reading and writing aim is in l1-presentational). Teacher note: a family prompt is always one of several and may be invented; no task asks where a family comes from, what work a parent does or what language is spoken at home. The heritage path is offered when a learner's work shows it (the teacher's judgment or the school's placement), never by asking the class who speaks Spanish at home. Descriptions are of a character, a picture or oneself, never a classmate's body or looks.

words: el horario; la clase; el lunes; hoy; mañana; hace sol; llueve; hace frío; el mapa; ¿qué día es hoy?
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Function: recognize and begin to understand familiar, well-supported words and phrases, cognates and borrowed words, one phrase at a time, and show it by pointing, matching, circling or marking a chart. Contexts: the same themes as the level, in highly predictable settings. Texts, authentic and from several places, with pictures: school timetables, classroom labels, weather maps and forecasts, calendars, a children's song, a short captioned photo set, a short spoken announcement of numbers or dates. Accuracy: needs pictures, gesture and repeats; rereading and relistening are planned, not a failure. In each unit the learner hears or reads one short authentic text twice and fills a picture chart (what day, what weather, what class) before the exchange uses the same facts. Heritage path: the learner reads the text aloud, then writes in Spanish what it says and checks the spelling against the text. Early-years companion (same target): picture books read aloud, songs with actions, total physical response games (stand up when you hear a color), answers by pointing.

words: yo soy; tengo; me gusta; mi clase favorita es; mi día; el formulario; el nombre; la fecha
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Function: present basic information about self or a character with words, lists and formula sentences, and fill a simple form (name, birthday, class schedule, likes). Text type: a labeled poster or slide, a short form, a spoken introduction of four to six practiced sentences. Grammar: the level's chunks used in a frame (Me llamo..., Tengo ... años, Me gusta... porque es...), adjectives after the noun with the ending noticed. Accuracy: accurate on rehearsed material, with spelling errors expected and worked on in short planned responses. In each unit the learner makes one product for an audience (a poster about my school day, a card introducing a made-up character, a weather report of a city), rehearses it with the frame, and gives it after the frame is withdrawn on the named day. Heritage path: writes a longer piece, edits it for accents and spelling, and writes the school register beside the home register. Early-years companion: listening and speaking aim at the level's target; reading and writing only as far as the child reads and writes in any language (copy and label). The companion says or sings a short rhyme, draws and labels a picture, shows a puppet introducing itself.

words: tú; usted; buenos días; buenas tardes; el apellido; el saludo; el año escolar
notes: Practices and the perspectives behind them, at Novice depth: greetings and courtesy (a handshake, a cheek kiss in some places and some families, buenos días to an adult), tú with a friend and usted with an adult, two surnames on a form in many places, how the school year and the school day run in several places (a school year from March to December in Chile and Argentina, double shifts in some schools). The learner greets a peer and an adult the fitting way in a short role play and reads two school calendars to say one way they differ. Each practice is shown from at least two Spanish-speaking places and as varied inside each place, never as what everyone in a country does. Heritage path: the learner names the greetings they use and adds the school-register form, as two registers, not right and wrong. Early-years companion (same target): greeting games and a calendar song. Teacher note: no single country is the default; practices are living and varied; no task asks about a learner's own family customs.

words: la canción; el juego; el mapa; el país; la ciudad; la bandera
notes: Products and what they mean to the people who make and use them, at Novice depth: children's songs and playground games from two or more places, a map of the places where Spanish is spoken (the 18 Spanish-speaking countries of Latin America, Puerto Rico, Spain and Equatorial Guinea, where it is an official language, and communities across the United States), school supplies and a school timetable as everyday products. The learner learns one game and one song and places on a map the cities the unit's texts come from. Early-years companion (same target): a song and a game, and pointing to places on a big map. Teacher note: no costume, sombrero or food-as-culture shortcut; flags only as map labels; a song is introduced with who sings it and where.

words: más; menos; son; el tiempo; la estación; el color; el norte; el sur
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-home-region (reading a political map to find places)
notes: Using Spanish to work with what other subjects already taught: say simple math facts (dos más tres son cinco), read a weather chart and the seasons, find places on a political map, name colors in an artwork. The learner makes a one-week weather chart for a city in another hemisphere and says what the weather is each day. The other subject is a pointer for the teacher, never an assumption: the unit reteaches the content it uses. Early-years companion (same target): counting songs, color games and a weather wheel.

words: el pronóstico; la temperatura; los grados; el verano; el invierno
notes: Getting information and another view from Spanish sources, at Novice depth: pick out two or three facts from a short authentic text with pictures (a weather page, a school website timetable, an infographic on a sport) and notice a view the learner did not expect (seasons reversed in the southern hemisphere, school in two shifts). The learner writes the facts on a chart in Spanish words and shares one surprise. Texts are chosen for the level, with support, not rewritten. Early-years companion (same target): a picture weather chart filled by pointing and stickers.

words: el cognado; el amigo falso; masculino; femenino; ¿?; ¡!; la mayúscula
cross_subject: ela:e2-sentences (what a sentence is, to compare word order)
notes: Comparing Spanish with English and other languages the learner knows, at Novice depth: cognates (la música, el animal) and a first false friend (la librería), nouns that carry gender, the adjective after the noun (la casa blanca), days and months in lower case, the opening ¿ and ¡ marks, the letters ñ and ü written correctly (SPA.Sounds.8, owned here). The learner sorts words on a comparison chart (same, looks the same but differs, different) and fixes punctuation in three short questions. Transfer from a home language is a reason, never a fault. Heritage path: the learner checks their own writing for the opening marks and accents, a spelling job, not a speaking drill. Early-years companion (same target): sorting picture cards of look-alike words, and drawing the ¿ and ¡ in the air.

words: igual; diferente; aquí; allá; también
notes: Comparing cultures at Novice depth: how people greet, how the school day and year run, and how names are written, across two Spanish-speaking places and the learner's own school community. The learner fills a three-column comparison chart and says one sentence with igual or diferente; no ranking and no verdict, and the learner's community is the school, not the family. Early-years companion (same target): a sorting game with pictures of greetings and school days. Teacher note: comparisons never set one place as normal and another as strange.

words: el letrero; la escuela; la biblioteca; bienvenidos
notes: Using Spanish beyond the lesson, inside the school and in public: label the classroom, greet school staff who have chosen to take part, share a song with a younger class, spot Spanish on public signs. The learner makes a set of labels or a welcome sign for a school space. Early-years companion (same target): singing for a younger class. Teacher note: no task needs a learner to find Spanish speakers outside school, use family members, or say whether the family speaks Spanish; two-way practice happens between people in the room. The course page and the family note name the part of this standard not claimed (use of Spanish with communities beyond the school).

words: puedo; mi meta; me gusta escuchar
notes: Lifelong learning at Novice depth: the learner judges their own work against our can-do paraphrases for the level (a learner-kept self-check, nothing recorded), sets one goal on a goal plan for the next unit, and chooses one song or children's program from public media in Spanish to enjoy. Early-years companion (same target): a sticker chart of songs the child can sing.

words: a; e; i; o; u; la hache; la jota; la elle; la eñe; la ve (la uve in Spain); el abecedario
notes: Sounds and spelling taught directly: the five vowel sounds, short and steady (SPA.Sounds.1), reading a new word aloud from its spelling (SPA.Sounds.2), and the letters that sound unlike English, silent h, j, ñ and v said like b, and the pair ll (SPA.Sounds.3). The learner builds a sound-spelling map with a key word for each sound and reads unseen names of cities aloud from it. The default variety is Latin American; other varieties are varieties, never errors. Heritage path: the sounds are known, so the learner works the other way, from sound to letter (h, ll and y, b and v), spelling words they say. Early-years companion (same target): vowel songs, letter games and clapping names.

words: ¿sí?; sí; ¿verdad?
notes: Raising or lowering the voice to mark a yes-no question or a statement (SPA.Sounds.9): the learner hears pairs (Tienes un perro. / ¿Tienes un perro?), marks the arrow on the sound-spelling map, and turns three statements into questions in the exchange. Early-years companion (same target): call-and-response songs where the voice goes up and down.

words: ¿quieres...?; ¿puedes...?; vamos a; ¿a qué hora?; ¿dónde está?; ¿cuánto cuesta?; estoy cansado / cansada; me duele; me levanto; lo siento; claro
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice High on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 1: the function moves from naming and listing to recombining practiced phrases into own short sentences and asking a few formula questions; the context widens to simple social situations and immediate needs; the text type is short present-tense sentences, sometimes incomplete; accuracy holds on familiar topics and misunderstandings are repaired by repeating or rephrasing. Themes: daily routine; home and the neighborhood (places in town, where they are); making plans and invitations (accept, decline, set a time); shopping for clothes or a gift with prices; how I feel and what hurts; sports, games and hobbies. Grammar the functions need: present of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs, ser, estar, tener, ir and hacer, stem-changing querer, poder and jugar, reflexive verbs for a routine, ir a with an infinitive for plans, gustar with a plural noun, estar for place and feeling, telling time, numbers to 1,000 for prices. In each unit the learner plans something with a partner from two different cards (two town maps, two weekly schedules) and agrees on a time and place, then does it again in text messages. On the Check day the pair uses a new card neither has seen: rehearsed language, unrehearsed content. Heritage path: writes the exchange with accents, and rewrites a message to a friend as a message to a teacher, naming the two registers. Early-years companion (same target): store play with toy money, invitation games, routine songs with actions. Teacher note: prompts about home and family may be invented; no task asks about family income or what a family can buy.

words: el anuncio; la oferta; la parada; la salida; a la derecha; a la izquierda; todo recto; el mensaje
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice High on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 1: the function moves from catching supported words to understanding short standard messages, brief instructions and simple informational texts where the words were taught, one sentence at a time, and often getting the main idea; contexts are practical needs and basic social settings; texts are short and connected; accuracy is uneven, with context doing much of the work. Grammar met as chunks: tú commands in directions (dobla, sigue, mira). Texts, authentic and from several places, Mexico among them: a store flyer, a transport sign and map, a short text message thread, a short interview with a young person about their routine, a song, recorded directions. In each unit the learner follows recorded directions on a map, picks out prices and times from an ad, and answers who, what, when and where questions on a short interview. Heritage path: reads a longer text of the same kind and writes a short summary in Spanish, checking spelling against the text. Early-years companion (same target): picture books with a repeated line, songs, follow-the-direction games.

words: primero; después; luego; por la mañana; por la tarde; la invitación; mi barrio; cerca de; lejos de
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Novice High on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Novice range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 1: the function moves from lists and formula lines to notes, short messages and a set of simple sentences that recombine learned language; the context is daily life; the text type is six to ten present-tense sentences spoken from notes or written, with sequence words, not yet sustained as a paragraph; accuracy may only partly carry the meaning on new topics. In each unit the learner makes one product: an invitation card with time, place and plan; a talk on my routine with pictures; a guide to a neighborhood, real or invented, with where places are. The frame is withdrawn on the unit's second Application day. Heritage path: writes a longer piece and edits for accents, b and v, h, and the written register. Early-years companion (same target): a picture diary of a day, told aloud with sequence words.

words: el almuerzo; la merienda; el transporte; el colectivo; el metro; la invitación; puntual
cross_subject: social-studies:ss2-culture-migration (what makes up a culture: its parts only)
notes: Harder than Level 1: from courtesy formulas to everyday practices of routine and town life, with the reason behind them. Practices: when the main meal of the day falls in different places and families, how people get around (a shared minibus, a metro, a bicycle), how markets and small shops work, how a birthday invitation and arriving on time work in different settings. The learner reads or hears two people from different places describe their day and says what each does and why it fits their setting. Each practice is shown as varied inside a place. Heritage path: describes a practice they know and adds where it is and is not common, with no claim that one way is the right one. Early-years companion (same target): role play of a market and a birthday. Teacher note: the lean points only at the parts of a culture; no task asks how or why a family moved.

words: la moneda; el billete; el mercado; la artesanía; el tejido; el artista
cross_subject: social-studies:ss4-regional-cultures (place names and buildings that Spanish speakers gave US regions)
notes: Harder than Level 1: from naming products to saying what a product is for and who makes it. Products: the coins and notes of several countries, transport maps, crafts explained by their makers (a weaver speaking about her textiles), a song of a sport or a city, Spanish place names in the United States, and Spanish-language radio, signs and murals in US cities today. The learner makes a short labeled display of three products with who makes them, where and what they are for. Early-years companion (same target): handling play coins and a craft shown by its maker. Teacher note: crafts are shown as living work by named communities in their own words, not as souvenirs; no costume or food-as-culture shortcut.

words: las dieciséis horas; el cambio; el cuerpo; la cabeza; el corazón; el horario
notes: Harder than Level 1: from naming facts in Spanish to doing a short task from another subject in Spanish. The learner reads a 24-hour timetable and works out travel times, converts a price between two currencies with a given rate, and names body parts and simple health facts from science. The unit reteaches the content it uses. Early-years companion (same target): body songs and clock games.

words: la guía; la información; según; el dato
notes: Harder than Level 1: from two or three facts to the main idea and a few details of a short informational text, and a second view. The learner reads a city transport guide or a short page on a sport from two places and fills a chart of facts, then says one way the two places see the same thing differently. Early-years companion (same target): a picture fact sort from a short read-aloud.

words: la terminación; -ción; -dad; -mente; el verbo; el sujeto
cross_subject: ela:e3-word-strategies (known word parts to work out a new word)
notes: Harder than Level 1: from noticing single words to comparing how the two languages build meaning. The verb ending carries the person, so the subject pronoun is often left out (hablo, hablas); reflexive verbs for a routine (me levanto); gender and number agreement across a noun phrase; cognate word parts (-ción and -tion, -dad and -ty, -mente and -ly) on a word-parts chart. The learner works out ten new cognates from their parts and finds two false friends in a text. Heritage path: works on agreement and spelling in writing, not the spoken forms they already have. Early-years companion (same target): matching word endings on picture cards.

words: en cambio; pero; los dos; más que; menos que
notes: Harder than Level 1: from single features to comparing whole routines. The learner compares the school day, getting around and the main meal across two Spanish-speaking places and the school community, in four or five sentences with pero and en cambio, and says why a practice fits its setting. No ranking and no verdict. Early-years companion (same target): a picture sort of two school days. Teacher note: the learner's own side of the chart is the school or an invented person, never a question about their home.

words: el cartel; el evento; la presentación; la radio
notes: Harder than Level 1: from labels to a short message for a school audience. The learner makes a bilingual poster for a school event or gives a short routine talk to a younger class, and finds one public Spanish-language radio program or broadcast to listen to. Early-years companion (same target): a class song or poster for a school event. Teacher note: the class product is the class's work, never a heritage speaker translating for others; no task needs contact outside school.

words: mi progreso; ya puedo; todavía no; quiero aprender
notes: Harder than Level 1: from one goal to tracking progress across a unit. The learner checks the can-do paraphrases at the start and end of each unit, writes in Spanish what they can do now, sets the next goal on the goal plan, and keeps a short list of songs or programs they chose to enjoy. Nothing is recorded or scored. Early-years companion (same target): a sticker chart of songs and stories the child can follow.

words: pero; perro; caro; carro; ca; que; qui; co; cu; za; ce; ci; ga; gue; gui; ja; ge; gi
notes: Sounds and spelling taught directly: the single tapped r and the trilled rr, heard and said in pairs (pero and perro) (SPA.Sounds.4), and choosing c, qu, z, g, gu or j to spell a sound before each vowel (SPA.Sounds.5), with the letters of Level 1 carried (~SPA.Sounds.3). The learner adds the spelling patterns to the sound-spelling map, sorts dictated words, and spells unseen words from the map. Heritage path: this is the core spelling work (c, s and z, g and j, ll and y) for a learner who hears the sounds already. Early-years companion (same target): tongue-twister songs for r and rr, said in play.

words: la sílaba; la sílaba tónica; ca-mi-sa; re-loj
notes: Splitting a word into syllables and saying the stressed syllable with the right stress (SPA.Sounds.6), so the written accent rule of Level 3 rests on it; question and statement intonation carried to longer questions with question words (~SPA.Sounds.9). The learner claps syllables, marks the stressed one in new words, and reads a short message aloud with question intonation. Early-years companion (same target): clapping syllables in names and songs.

words: ¿me podría decir...?; quisiera; ¿cuánto cuesta el boleto?; ¿hay...?; ¿qué hiciste?; fui; compré; ¿cómo se dice?; o sea; es decir; la receta médica; la habitación
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Low on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 2: the function is first creating with language: starting and closing a short conversation or written exchange in a straightforward situation, asking and answering simple questions, and finishing a simple transaction with a patient partner; contexts widen to travel and getting around (tickets, lodging, directions), ordering food, a visit to a pharmacy or clinic, school life and interests, community places and services, media and technology habits; the text type is single sentences of the learner's own, sometimes joined with y, pero or porque, and first short answers about what happened; accuracy: understood by a partner used to learners, with pauses, rewording and repetition. Strategies taught: ask for clarification, restate, talk around a missing word (circumlocution), simplify. Grammar the functions need: the preterite of regular -ar verbs and of ir and ser in the first and second person for what happened (slips expected), the imperfect met only as chunks (era, había, tenía), direct object pronouns (indirect ones only in gustar-type chunks), usted and tú affirmative commands for polite requests and directions, comparisons, the present progressive, quisiera. In each unit the learner completes a transaction with a partner who holds the other half of the information (a traveler and a clerk with different cards, two people planning a trip from two timetables) and does an unrehearsed version on the Check day. Heritage path: works on the formal written exchange (an email asking a service for information) and on spelling, never as the partner who supplies the answers. Teacher note: a trip or a home in a task may be invented; no task asks about a family's travel, money or legal status.

words: el aviso; la noticia; el andén; el vuelo; la idea principal; el detalle; había una vez; al final
cross_subject: ela:e5-figurative (simile and metaphor in a song or poem)
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Low on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 2: the function is getting some information, often the main idea, from short simple connected texts and sentence-length speech, and following announcements, instructions and directions on taught topics; contexts are everyday personal and social settings; texts are short, simple and highly predictable description and narration; accuracy is uneven, with rereading or relistening needed; formal and informal are told apart in simple phrases. Texts, authentic and from several places, Mexico among them: a station or airport announcement, a travel blog post, a short news item for young readers, a short simple story, a song or poem with a simile, a recipe or a pharmacy leaflet as a text type. In each unit the learner fills a story map or a main-idea chart from one text and answers detail questions in Spanish, reading or listening twice. Heritage path: reads a longer authentic text of the same kind, notes words of a different register, and writes a short summary.

words: el fin de semana pasado; ayer; cuando era niño / niña; antes; ahora; porque; también; pero; en mi opinión
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Low on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Writing aims one sublevel below speaking (Novice High at Level 3). Harder than Level 2: the function is presenting own information and preferences on familiar topics in sentences of the learner's own, and a first short retelling of a past event with taught past forms; contexts are home, routine, interests, food, shopping and travel; the text type is six to ten simple sentences with a few connectors (porque, también, pero), or a two minute talk with visuals; accuracy: present-tense patterns controlled, past forms limited to the taught ones and attempted with errors. In each unit the learner makes one product: a description of a place compared with another, a simple narration of a past weekend or trip (real or invented) planned on a story map, a short guide to a community service. The paragraph frame is introduced here, and the sentence frame is withdrawn on the unit's first Application day. Heritage path: drafts and revises a longer composition for spelling, accents and the school register.

words: vos; la sobremesa; el regateo; la farmacia; el turno; la costumbre
notes: Harder than Level 2: from describing a practice to explaining the perspective behind it, with fitting expressions in everyday exchanges. Practices: forms of address (tú, usted and vos, with voseo in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America, and in parts of Colombia, Chile and other places, as a variety), lingering at the table after a meal in some places, bargaining at some markets and not in shops, the pharmacist as a first stop for a minor illness in some places, public transport etiquette. The learner explains in Spanish why a practice makes sense in its setting, using what a person from that place says about it. Heritage path: compares the forms of address they use with the ones in the texts, as varieties. Teacher note: practices are shown from several places and as changing, with people speaking for themselves.

words: la cumbia; la salsa; el mural; la palabra indígena; el náhuatl; el quechua; la leyenda
notes: Harder than Level 2: from what a product is for to what it shows about the people who value it. Products: music from several places (cumbia, salsa, son and their African roots, and newer styles) with what the music means to its listeners, murals and public art (among them murals in US cities made by Mexican American and Puerto Rican artists), stories and legends told by their communities, words Spanish took from Indigenous languages (chocolate and tomate from Nahuatl, cancha from Quechua). The learner presents one product with its place, its makers and what it means to them. Teacher note: colonial history and Indigenous languages are named where they bear on the product, with the community's own words first; no costume or food-as-culture shortcut.

words: el clima; la región; la montaña; la costa; la encuesta; el gráfico; el porcentaje
notes: Harder than Level 2: from a short task to using Spanish to learn some content of another subject. The learner compares climates and regions of two Spanish-speaking places with a map and a climate chart (geography and science), and runs a short class survey on media habits and reports it as a graph with percentages (math). The unit reteaches the content it uses.

words: el punto de vista; la fuente; el artículo; comparar
notes: Harder than Level 2: from facts to two points of view. The learner reads or hears two short Spanish texts from different places on the same topic (city transport, a festival, school uniforms; in at least one unit, one of the two is a Spanish-language source from the United States) and writes three sentences on how the views differ and one on what the learner learned that an English source would not show.

words: el pretérito; ser; estar; el pronombre; actual; realizar; la carpeta; embarazada
cross_subject: ela:e6-word-strategies (Greek and Latin roots shared by the two languages)
notes: Harder than Level 2: from word parts to grammar that works differently. The learner compares ser and estar with English to be, the preterite with the English past, object pronouns placed before the verb (lo compré), and shared Latin roots on the word-parts chart, and keeps a list of false friends met in texts (actual, realizar, carpeta, embarazada). Transfer is named as a reason. Heritage path: compares home and school forms (for example an everyday form beside the written one) as registers, not errors.

words: la perspectiva; depende de; en cambio; me sorprendió
notes: Harder than Level 2: from comparing routines to comparing the perspectives behind them. The learner compares a practice (address forms, a health habit, getting around) across two places and the school community, explains why each fits its setting, and names one generalization that would be unfair. No ranking. Teacher note: the learner's own side is the school, a public source or an invented person, never a question about home.

words: la guía; el folleto; el público; la emisora; el programa
notes: Harder than Level 2: from a short message to a product a school audience uses. The learner makes, with the class, a short Spanish guide to a school space or event, or a talk for a younger Spanish class, and notices Spanish in the local public world (signs, library books, public broadcasts) by observing, never by approaching people. Teacher note: a bilingual product is class work; a heritage speaker is not the class translator. Optional, never required, arranged by the school and never through the site: a class-to-class letter exchange with a Spanish-speaking class, or a guest the school invites; the course page offers it as a way toward the part of standard 5.1 the course does not claim.

words: la estrategia; la meta; aprendí; me ayuda
notes: Harder than Level 2: from tracking progress to choosing strategies. The learner rates their own can-do paraphrases per mode, names the strategy that helped (rereading, talking around a word, a word bank), sets a goal on the goal plan, and chooses a Spanish-language song, program or book for young readers to follow over the unit.

words: la tilde; aguda; llana; esdrújula; sí; si; él; el; tú; tu; qué; que; habló; hablo
notes: Using the written accent to mark stress and to tell sí from si, él from el (SPA.Sounds.7), resting on the stress and spelling work of Level 2 (~SPA.Sounds.5, ~SPA.Sounds.6). The learner applies the rule (stress on the last syllable, the one before it, or earlier), adds accents to question words, and hears the difference between hablo and habló, where the accent carries the time. Heritage path: the main written-accent work, on their own compositions.

words: la variedad; el acento; el seseo; el yeísmo
notes: Recognizing regional sounds as varieties of Spanish, not errors (SPA.Sounds.11): s said where much of Spain says th, in all of Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of southern Spain; ll and y said alike in most places, and as sh or zh in Buenos Aires and Montevideo; a final s softened in the Caribbean and elsewhere. Hearing words run together at natural speed, vowel to vowel and consonant to vowel, as speakers link them (SPA.Sounds.10, owned here because the Level 3 listening rests on it). The learner hears short authentic clips from several places and matches each feature to its region on a map. Teacher note: no variety is the correct one; a learner's own accent or home variety is never corrected as an error of meaning.

words: mientras; de repente; cuando llegué; iré; me gustaría; espero que; es importante que; ¿qué pasó?; lo que pasa es que; propongo
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 3: the learner handles a variety of uncomplicated tasks and social situations, keeps a conversation going with a range of questions, tells briefly what happened and what will happen, and copes with a small taught change in a plan (a changed time, a wrong order) using practiced phrases; contexts are school, recreation, interests and community matters handled concretely; the text type is strings of sentences on familiar topics; accuracy: generally understood, with pauses, rewording and self-correction, and slips when the time frame changes. Themes: community and public life (the environment, volunteering, transport in a city); school, future plans and work interests; arts, media and technology; health and well-being; travel stories. Grammar the functions need: preterite and imperfect both used in a story, slips expected; the future, the conditional and the present subjunctive met as chunks (iré, me gustaría, quiero que, es importante que, ojalá, no te preocupes), not as paradigms; relative que and donde. Beyond Level 4: the full preterite and imperfect contrast and the productive subjunctive. In each unit the learner solves a problem with a partner who holds different information (two witnesses of an event, two planners with different constraints), unrehearsed on the Check day. Heritage path: leads nothing for the class; works on the formal register in a debate or an interview, and on spelling in written exchanges. Teacher note: community topics stay concrete and local; no task asks about immigration, legal status, family income or home language use.

words: el reportaje; la entrevista; el pódcast; el cuento; el narrador; la opinión; según el autor; deducir
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Harder than Level 3: the learner gets the main idea and some details of simple connected texts on familiar topics, infers a new word from context, and tells a stated opinion from a fact; contexts are personal, social and community topics the learner brings knowledge to. Texts, authentic and from several places: a short article for young readers, an interview, a podcast segment, a short story by a writer from the region studied, a documentary clip with captions. In each unit the learner maps the story or the article (events in order, what changed, the opinion stated) and answers inference questions in Spanish. Heritage path: reads a full-length authentic text of the same kind and writes a summary in the school register.

words: el párrafo; para empezar; para terminar; el resumen; por eso; por lo tanto; en primer lugar; finalmente; recomiendo que
notes: Exit aim for this mode: Intermediate Mid on the taught themes of the level, the proficiency estimate the course aims toward; the checks judge performance on the taught themes in the Intermediate range and never give a rating (no proficiency interview). Writing aims one sublevel below speaking (Intermediate Low at Level 4). Harder than Level 3: the function is strings of connected sentences on familiar topics: telling a past event, preterite and imperfect both attempted, with slips when the time frame shifts, summarizing a school or personal experience, and proposing a change with taught chunks (recomiendo que, es importante que, iré); contexts are school, recreation, interests and the community; the text type is a short composition of ten to fifteen sentences with an opening and a close, a first paragraph attempted, or a three minute talk; accuracy: understood by a reader used to learners, with weak spots when time frames shift. In each unit the learner drafts, revises with a checklist and presents one product: a story of a memorable day (real or invented), a summary of a project, a proposal for a school or community improvement. The paragraph frame is withdrawn on the unit's first Application day. Heritage path: writes a longer piece with full control of accents and the formal register, revising against the same checklist.

words: la minga; la comunidad; el voluntariado; la identidad; hispano; latino; latine; el guaraní
notes: Harder than Level 3: from explaining one practice to describing how practices carry shared values in a community. Practices: shared community work (the minga in the Andes), volunteering and civic life, youth culture, languages living side by side (Spanish with Guaraní in Paraguay, Quechua in Peru, Catalan, Basque and Galician in Spain, and Afro-descendant communities on the Caribbean and Pacific coasts), and the names people choose for themselves (Hispanic, Latino, Latine; choices differ). The learner explains a practice and its perspective in a paragraph, quoting a speaker from that community. Teacher note: names for people use the term each community uses and say that choices differ; no task asks a learner which term fits them.

words: el muralismo; el poema; la película; el escritor; la escritora; la obra
notes: Harder than Level 3: from presenting a product to interpreting what it says about its time and place. Products: a short story or poem, a film or short film, public murals, an architecture style, a music movement, a writer or musician from Equatorial Guinea or the Caribbean, each from a named place and time. The learner interprets one product in a short paragraph and links it to a perspective of the people who made it. Teacher note: religious holidays and rites in a product are described, never observed; colonial history is named with the community's own words first.

words: el medio ambiente; el agua; el río; el contacto; la historia; la lengua indígena
notes: Harder than Level 3: from learning some content to working through a short inquiry from another subject in Spanish. The learner studies a science or history topic of a Spanish-speaking region (water in a dry region, how mountains and coasts shaped where languages meet) from Spanish texts and presents what they found. The unit reteaches the content it uses.

words: investigar; la pregunta; citar; la fuente; el punto de vista
notes: Harder than Level 3: from comparing two views to a short research question. The learner asks a question, finds and cites two or three Spanish-language sources from different places, notes each source's view, and writes a short paragraph on what the sources agree and differ on.

words: el imperfecto; el subjuntivo; el modo; el registro; el modismo; la traducción literal
notes: Harder than Level 3: from single forms to how a whole system differs. The learner compares preterite and imperfect with English simple past, used to and was doing; the subjunctive mood with English, which marks the same idea other ways; registers (tú, usted, vos); and idioms that break under literal translation. Heritage path: compares registers in their own writing and names when each fits.

words: la suposición; el estereotipo; desde otro punto de vista
notes: Harder than Level 3: from comparing perspectives to examining the learner's own assumptions. The learner compares how two places and the school community handle a concrete public matter (recycling, public transport, a shared space), names one assumption they held before, and says how the texts changed it. Teacher note: no ranking; stereotypes are named only to take them apart.

words: el servicio; el proyecto; la campaña; el público
notes: Harder than Level 3: from a guide to a project with a real school audience. The learner, with the class, carries out a short Spanish-language project for the school (a public-service poster campaign, a presentation to a younger class, a bilingual event program) and follows public Spanish-language media on a topic. Teacher note: no task needs contact with people outside school; class products are never a heritage speaker translating. Optional, never required, arranged by the school and never through the site: a class-to-class letter exchange with a Spanish-speaking class, or a guest the school invites; the course page offers it as a way toward the part of standard 5.1 the course does not claim.

words: seguir aprendiendo; el trabajo; útil; mi plan
notes: Harder than Level 3: from strategies within the course to a plan beyond it. The learner rates the can-do paraphrases per mode for the whole level, writes a plan for keeping the language (media they choose, a word bank, a reading list), and notes where the language is used in work that interests them.

words: la sinalefa; ¿qué es esto?; mi hermano; lo hago
notes: Harder than Level 3: reading a paragraph aloud with linking and stress, and following connected speech at natural speed across varieties (~SPA.Sounds.10, ~SPA.Sounds.11): vowel meets vowel across words, a final consonant joins the next vowel. The learner follows clips from several varieties, reads a paragraph aloud with linking and stress, and keeps written accents right in future, conditional and subjunctive forms (~SPA.Sounds.7).
